text: Day one of a new project, the whiteboard filling up. The Gītā's sāttvic doer has zeal (utsāha) and steadiness (dhṛti), clings to nothing, and does not speak of 'I'. The whiteboard is the zeal; the verse adds steadiness, and no 'I'. Zeal without the 'I'? (Bhagavad Gītā 18.26)

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original: muktasaṅgo'nahaṃvādī dhṛtyutsāhasamanvitaḥ|siddhyasiddhyornirvikāraḥ kartā sāttvika ucyate
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: the agent who is free of attachment, does not speak of 'I' (anahaṃvādin), is endowed with steadiness (dhṛti) and zeal (utsāha), and is unchanged in success and failure, is called sāttvic.

text: A report goes out with a mistake on page two. The inflow of karma from an act differs, the Tattvārtha says, by intensity or mildness, and by knowing or not knowing. The Jain text weighs whether it was done knowingly. How much does the mistake weigh? (Tattvārthasūtra 6.6)

cite.title: Tattvārthasūtra
cite.original: tīvra-maṃda-jñātājñāta-bhāvādhikaraṇa-vīrya-viśeṣebhyastadviśeṣaḥ
cite.paraphrase: The differences within it arise from intensity (tīvra) or mildness (manda), doing knowingly or unknowingly (jñāta-ajñāta), the disposition (bhāva), the substratum (adhikaraṇa) and the energy (vīrya).

text:
Praise in the meeting, and the wish to hear it again.
An old text puts it this way: Acting without clinging, the Gītā says, one is not stained by sin (pāpa), as water does not stain a lotus leaf. (Bhagavad Gītā 5.10)
Kṛṣṇa: one who acts, placing actions in Brahman (brahmaṇy ādhāya) and abandoning attachment (saṅga), is not stained by sin (pāpa), as a lotus leaf is not stained by water. The acting goes on; the attachment is what is abandoned.
The leaf sits in water all day; the stain comes with clinging, not acting.
Sit with that.

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original:
brahmaṇyādhāya karmāṇi saṅgaṃ tyaktvā karoti yaḥ|
lipyate na sa pāpena padmapatramivāmbhasā
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: one who acts, placing actions in Brahman (brahmaṇy ādhāya) and abandoning attachment (saṅga), is not stained by sin (pāpa), as a lotus leaf is not stained by water.

text:
A new colleague asks how the system works, on the busiest day.
An old text puts it this way: Concealing knowledge, envy and obstructing it, the Tattvārtha says, bring in knowledge-obscuring karma. (Tattvārthasūtra 6.10)
The sūtra names six acts with regard to knowledge and perception: spite (pradoṣa), concealment (nihnava), envy (mātsarya), obstruction (antarāya), disrespect and injury. They are the inflow of the karmas that obscure knowledge and perception.
A vague answer would be concealment (nihnava) on the Jain list, and the karma it names falls on the one who conceals.
Sit with that.

cite.title: Tattvārthasūtra
cite.original: tatpradoṣa-nihnava-mātsaryāntarāyāsādanopaghātā jñāna-darśanāvaraṇayoḥ
cite.paraphrase: Spite (pradoṣa), concealment (nihnava), envy (mātsarya), obstruction (antarāya), disrespect (āsādana) and injury (upaghāta) with regard to them (tat: knowledge and perception) are the inflow of the knowledge-obscuring and perception-obscuring karmas (jñāna-āvaraṇa, darśana-āvaraṇa).

text:
A message from the manager: 'Quick call?' and nothing more.
An old text has a word for this.
For truthful speech, the Tattvārtha says, give up anger, greed, fear and joking.
Source: Tattvārthasūtra 7.5
Before replying, the Jain text asks which is speaking: anger, greed, fear or the joke.
Which one is typing?
A message from the manager: 'Quick call?' and nothing more. For truthful speech, the Tattvārtha says, give up anger, greed, fear and joking. Before replying, the Jain text asks which is speaking: anger, greed, fear or the joke. Source: Tattvārthasūtra 7.5.

cite.title: Tattvārthasūtra
cite.original: krodha-lobha-bhīrutva-hāsya-pratyākhyānānyanuvīci-bhāṣaṇaṃ ca pañca
cite.paraphrase: For truthfulness: giving up anger (krodha), greed (lobha), fear (bhīrutva) and laughter (hāsya), and speaking in conformity (anuvīci-bhāṣaṇa): these five.

text:
The team board shows everyone's delays in red.
An old text has a word for this.
Do not look for others' faults, the Dhammapada says, or at what they have done and left undone; look at one's own.
Source: Dhammapada 50
The verse turns that look around, to one's own deeds.
What did today leave undone?
The team board shows everyone's delays in red. Do not look for others' faults, the Dhammapada says, or at what they have done and left undone; look at one's own. The verse turns that look around, to one's own deeds. Source: Dhammapada 50.

cite.title: Dhammapada
cite.original: Na paresaṁ vilomāni, na paresaṁ katākataṁ; Attanova avekkheyya, katāni akatāni ca.
cite.paraphrase: One should not look for the faults of others, nor at what others have done and left undone; one should look at one's own deeds done and undone.

text:
[on screen: A colleague presents your idea in the meeting as their own.] A colleague presents your idea in the meeting as their own.
[on screen: Bhagavad Gītā 12.18] There is an old text that says it plainly. Dear to Kṛṣṇa is one who is the same toward enemy and friend, in honour and in dishonour.
Here is what the passage says, closely: Kṛṣṇa describes the one dear to him: the same toward enemy and friend, in honour and dishonour, in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and freed from attachment (saṅga).
The verse lists enemy and friend beside honour and dishonour: one evenness for all.
The old texts are often this plain. They name the thing, and leave the seeing to the reader.
Where the text stops: it describes what happens; it does not promise a result.
[on screen: Sit with that.] Sit with that.

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original: samaḥ śatrau ca mitre ca tathā mānāpamānayoḥ|śītoṣṇasukhaduḥkheṣu samaḥ saṅgavivarjitaḥ
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: the same toward enemy and friend, and likewise in honour and dishonour; the same in cold and heat, pleasure and pain; freed from attachment (saṅga) —

text:
[on screen: A ninety-minute meeting, and one sentence in it mattered.] A ninety-minute meeting, and one sentence in it mattered.
[on screen: Dhammapada 100] There is an old text that says it plainly. One meaningful word that calms the hearer, the Dhammapada says, is better than a thousand meaningless ones.
Here is what the passage says, closely: Even a thousand utterances (vācā) made up of meaningless words, the verse says, are surpassed by one meaningful word (atthapada), on hearing which one is calmed.
The verse weighs words by meaning, not by number.
The old texts are often this plain. They name the thing, and leave the seeing to the reader.
Where the text stops: it describes what happens; it does not promise a result.
[on screen: Which sentence was it?] Which sentence was it?

cite.title: Dhammapada
cite.original: Sahassamapi ce vācā, anatthapadasaṁhitā; Ekaṁ atthapadaṁ seyyo, yaṁ sutvā upasammati.
cite.paraphrase: Even a thousand utterances (vācā) made up of meaningless words are surpassed by one meaningful word (atthapada) on hearing which one is calmed (upasammati).

text:
1. The scene (about 2 min). Points: The spreadsheet is finally right, and no one will notice. Stay with the moment before judging it.
2. The teaching (about 2 min). Points: Dear to Kṛṣṇa is one who is capable (dakṣa) and without expectation (anapekṣa), pure and untroubled. Source: Bhagavad Gītā 12.16.
3. Reading closely (about 2 min). Points: Kṛṣṇa lists the marks of one dear to him: without expectation, pure, capable, impartial, rid of distress, relinquishing every undertaking, and devoted to him. Capability and expecting nothing stand in the same line. Say only what the passage says.
4. The link (about 2 min). Points: Capable, yes. The verse adds the other half: expecting nothing back.
5. Where the text stops (about 1 min). Points: Where the text stops: it describes what happens; it does not promise a result.
6. Close (about 1 min). Points: Can both be held at once?

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original: anapekṣaḥ śucirdakṣa udāsīno gatavyathaḥ|sarvārambhaparityāgī yo madbhaktaḥ sa me priyaḥ
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: without expectation (anapekṣa), pure (śuci), capable (dakṣa), impartial (udāsīna), rid of distress (gata-vyatha), relinquishing every undertaking (sarvārambha-parityāgin) — who is devoted to me, he is dear to me.

text: A window seat, and each passing car pulls the thought elsewhere. For one whose thoughts run about, the Visuddhimagga says, a wide view feeds the running. The text is practical: a sweeping view gives racing thought more to chase. What is the view feeding? (Visuddhimagga 3.p110)

cite.title: Visuddhimagga
cite.original:
nisinnassa ārāmavanapokkharaṇīrāmaṇeyyakāni gāmaniga-  
majanapadapaṭipāṭiyā1 nīlobhāsā ca pabbatā paññāyanti,  
taṃ na vaṭṭati| taṃ hi vitakkavidhāvanass'; eva paccayo  
hoti| tasmā gambhīre darīmukhe2 vanapaṭicchanne hatthi-  
kucchipabbhāra-mahindaguhāsadise senāsane vasitabbaṃ|  
ārammaṇam pi 'ssa vipulaṃ na vaṭṭati; tādisaṃ hi vitakka-  
vasena sandhāvanāya3 paccayo hoti, parittaṃ pana vaṭṭati|  
sesaṃ rāgacaritassa vuttasadisam evā ti idaṃ vitakkacaritassa  
sappāyaṃ|
cite.paraphrase: What suits the speculative person. A lodging that opens toward a direction where, as he sits, pleasant parks, groves and lotus ponds, a succession of villages, towns and districts, and blue-shining mountains can be seen does not suit him, because it becomes a cause of his thoughts running about. So he should live in a lodging such as a deep cave-mouth screened by forest, like the Hatthikucchi Overhang or Mahinda's Cave. A large object is not suitable, for it would be a cause of the running about of thought; a small one is suitable. The rest is as said for the greedy person.

text: Halfway through a sentence, the mind already three topics on. The Satipaṭṭhāna asks one to know a scattered mind (vikkhitta) as 'scattered'. No fixing here: knowing 'scattered' is itself the practice. What is the mind like at this moment? (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta mn10:34)

cite.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
cite.original: 3. Cittānupassanā Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu citte cittānupassī viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sarāgaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘sarāgaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vītarāgaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vītarāgaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Sadosaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘sadosaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vītadosaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vītadosaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Samohaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘samohaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vītamohaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vītamohaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Saṅkhittaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘saṅkhittaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vikkhittaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vikkhittaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Mahaggataṁ vā cittaṁ ‘mahaggataṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Amahaggataṁ vā cittaṁ ‘amahaggataṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Sauttaraṁ vā cittaṁ ‘sauttaraṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Anuttaraṁ vā cittaṁ ‘anuttaraṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Samāhitaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘samāhitaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Asamāhitaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘asamāhitaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Vimuttaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘vimuttaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti. Avimuttaṁ vā cittaṁ ‘avimuttaṁ cittan’ti pajānāti.
cite.paraphrase: Contemplation of mind (citta). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating mind in mind. Here he knows a mind with lust (sarāga) as 'mind with lust', and a mind without lust as 'mind without lust'; a mind with hatred (sadosa) and without hatred; a mind with delusion (samoha) and without delusion; a contracted (saṅkhitta) mind and a scattered (vikkhitta) mind; an exalted (mahaggata) and an unexalted mind; a surpassable (sauttara) and an unsurpassable (anuttara) mind; a concentrated (samāhita) and an unconcentrated mind; a liberated (vimutta) and an unliberated mind.

text:
An angry message, deleted, then retyped in the head.
An old text puts it this way: Among the supports of non-violence, the Tattvārtha lists restraint of speech and of mind (mano-gupti). (Tattvārthasūtra 7.4)
The sūtra gives five contemplations that keep the vow of non-violence steady: restraint of speech (vāg-gupti), restraint of mind (mano-gupti), careful walking, care in picking up and putting down, and looking at food and drink.
The Jain list puts guarding the mind right beside guarding speech.
Where is the message now?

cite.title: Tattvārthasūtra
cite.original: vāṅmanoguptīryādānanikṣepaṇa-samityālokita-pāna-bhojanāni pañca
cite.paraphrase: For non-violence: restraint of speech (vāg-gupti), restraint of mind (mano-gupti), careful walking (īryā-samiti), careful picking up and putting down (ādāna-nikṣepaṇa-samiti), and looking at food and drink (ālokita-pāna-bhojana): these five.

text:
Before a trip, everything that could go wrong gets rehearsed.
An old text has a word for this.
A mind held steady, the Gītā says, is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker.
Source: Bhagavad Gītā 6.19
The lamp is not put out; it still burns. Only the wind drops.
What is the wind, in the rehearsal?
Before a trip, everything that could go wrong gets rehearsed. A mind held steady, the Gītā says, is like a lamp in a windless place that does not flicker. The lamp is not put out; it still burns. Only the wind drops. Source: Bhagavad Gītā 6.19.

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original:
yathā dīpo nivātastho neṅgate sopamā smṛtā|
yogino yatacittasya yuñjato yogamātmanaḥ
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: 'As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker' — that is the simile handed down (smṛtā) for the yogin of restrained mind (citta) who practises the yoga of the self.

text:
Stuck at a red light, planning three conversations at once.
An old text has a word for this.
Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, Kṛṣṇa says, bring it back from there.
Source: Bhagavad Gītā 6.26
No verdict on the wandering; the instruction is the return.
Where has it gone right now?
Stuck at a red light, planning three conversations at once. Wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, Kṛṣṇa says, bring it back from there. No verdict on the wandering; the instruction is the return. Source: Bhagavad Gītā 6.26.

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original:
yato yato niścarati manaścañcalamasthiram|
tatastato niyamyaitadātmanyeva vaśaṃ nayet
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: wherever the restless (cañcala), unsteady mind wanders off, from there he should restrain it and bring it back under control in the self alone.

text:
[on screen: Arguing again, at the sink, with a remark from last spring.] Arguing again, at the sink, with a remark from last spring.
[on screen: Visuddhimagga 9.p301] There is an old text that says it plainly. Since states are momentary, the Visuddhimagga says, what did the harm has ceased: with whom is one angry now?
Here is what the passage says, closely: These are the last verses for one whose resentment will not settle. States are momentary, so the aggregates by which the disagreeable thing was done have ceased: with whom is one now angry?
Here the question is literal: those moments have ceased.
Notice what the text does and does not say. It describes what happens in the mind; it promises nothing.
Where the text stops: it describes what happens; it does not promise a result.
[on screen: With whom, now?] With whom, now?

cite.title: Visuddhimagga
cite.original:
khaṇikattā ca dhammānaṃ, yehi khandhehi te kataṃ  
          amanāpaṃ niruddhā te kassa dānī 'dha kujjhasi?  
          dukkhaṃ karoti yo yassa, taṃ vinā kassa so kare;  
          sayam pi dukkhahetu tvam iti kiṃ tassa kujjhasī ti?
cite.paraphrase: The last verses: since states are momentary, the aggregates by which the disagreeable thing was done to you have ceased: with whom are you now angry? He who does harm to another does it to someone; without that other he could not; and you yourself are a cause of suffering, so why are you angry with him?

text:
[on screen: The same worry, back for the twentieth time today.] The same worry, back for the twentieth time today.
[on screen: Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda Kārikā, Āgamaśāstra) 3.41] There is an old text that says it plainly. Restraining the mind, Gauḍapāda says, is like emptying the ocean drop by drop with a grass-tip, without weariness.
Here is what the passage says, closely: Gauḍapāda's simile: as the ocean might be emptied drop by drop with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, so the restraint of the mind is to be achieved without weariness (aparikheda).
He admits the size of the task. His word for the manner is without weariness (aparikheda).
The old texts are often this plain. They name the thing, and leave the seeing to the reader.
Where the text stops: it describes what happens; it does not promise a result.
[on screen: Sit with that.] Sit with that.

cite.title: Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda Kārikā, Āgamaśāstra)
cite.original: utseka udadher yadvat kuśāgreṇaikabindunā / manaso nigrahas tadvad bhaved aparikhedataḥ
cite.paraphrase: As the ocean might be emptied drop by drop with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, so the restraint of the mind should be achieved without weariness (aparikheda).

text: Brushing teeth at midnight, only half there. The Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna asks for clear knowing (sampajāna) in every act, falling asleep and waking among them. Sleeping sits in the list beside eating, asked only to be known. What is known, at this hour? (Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta dn22:4)

cite.title: Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta
cite.original: 1.3. Kāyānupassanāsampajānapabba Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hoti, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī hoti, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī hoti, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hoti, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī hoti, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti. Iti ajjhattaṁ vā …pe… Evampi kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati. Sampajānapabbaṁ niṭṭhitaṁ.
cite.paraphrase: Third section on the body: clear comprehension (sampajāna). A monk acts with clear comprehension in going forward and back, looking ahead and away, bending and stretching, wearing robes and carrying bowl, eating, drinking, chewing and tasting, defecating and urinating, and in walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking and keeping silent. The refrain is abbreviated (…pe…) and the section ends.

text: A power cut at night, and the flat goes fully dark. When sun, moon and fire are gone and speech is silent, the Bṛhadāraṇyaka says, the self is a person's light. Janaka asks the same question, one light at a time. What is still lit? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.2-6)

cite.title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
cite.paraphrase: Janaka asks: what is the light of a person? The sun; by its light one sits, goes out, works and returns. When the sun has set? The moon. When both have set? Fire. When fire has gone out? Speech. When speech too is silent? The self (ātman) is his light; by the light of the self he sits, goes out, works and returns.

text:
Past midnight, the room dark and the mind not.
An old text puts it this way: Yoga is not for one who eats too much or not at all, the Gītā says, nor one who sleeps too much or too little. (Bhagavad Gītā 6.16)
Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna: yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all; not for one given to too much sleep, nor for one who keeps always awake.
The verse sets no hours; it names only the two edges.
Sit with that.

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original:
nātyaśnatastu yogo'sti na caikāntamanaśnataḥ|
na cātisvapnaśīlasya jāgrato naiva cārjuna
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all, nor for one given to too much sleep, nor for one who keeps (always) awake, Arjuna.

text:
A nap that ran two hours, and waking unsure what day it is.
An old text puts it this way: The Tattvārtha lists kinds of sleep and drowsiness among the karmas that veil perception (darśana-āvaraṇa). (Tattvārthasūtra 8.7)
The perception-obscuring karma has nine kinds. Four veil visual, non-visual, clairvoyant and omniscient perception. Five are forms of sleep: sleep (nidrā), deep sleep, drowsiness (pracalā), heavy drowsiness, and sleepwalking (styānagṛddhi).
The Jain text files every grade of sleep under what veils seeing. It describes; it does not scold.
What was veiled, for those two hours?

cite.title: Tattvārthasūtra
cite.original: cakṣuracakṣuravadhikevalānāṃ nidrā-nidrānidrā-pracalā-pracalāpracalā-styānagṛddhayaśca
cite.paraphrase: The perception-obscuring karma has nine: the obscurations of visual (cakṣus), non-visual (acakṣus), clairvoyant (avadhi) and omniscient (kevala) perception, and sleep (nidrā), deep sleep (nidrānidrā), drowsiness (pracalā), heavy drowsiness (pracalāpracalā) and somnambulism (styānagṛddhi).

text:
Sitting awake at dawn in a silent room.
An old text has a word for this.
In deep sleep the mind is absorbed, Gauḍapāda says; restrained, it is not, and that is fearless brahman.
Source: Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda Kārikā, Āgamaśāstra) 3.35
Two stillnesses; deep sleep is not the one he points to.
And the difference?
Sitting awake at dawn in a silent room. In deep sleep the mind is absorbed, Gauḍapāda says; restrained, it is not, and that is fearless brahman. Two stillnesses; deep sleep is not the one he points to. Source: Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda Kārikā, Āgamaśāstra) 3.35.

cite.title: Māṇḍūkya Kārikā (Gauḍapāda Kārikā, Āgamaśāstra)
cite.original: līyate hi suṣupte tan nigṛhītaṃ na līyate / tad eva nirbhayaṃ brahma jñānalokaṃ samantataḥ
cite.paraphrase: That [mind] is absorbed (līyate) in deep sleep; when restrained it is not absorbed; that itself is fearless brahman, with the light of knowledge on every side.

text:
The morning's first words: 'I slept like a stone'.
An old text has a word for this.
Waking, one says 'I slept deeply, my limbs are heavy', Vyāsa notes; sleep is remembered, so it is a cognition.
Source: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra) 1.10
The stone-like night left a memory. For Vyāsa, that memory is the evidence.
What was remembered?
The morning's first words: 'I slept like a stone'. Waking, one says 'I slept deeply, my limbs are heavy', Vyāsa notes; sleep is remembered, so it is a cognition. The stone-like night left a memory. For Vyāsa, that memory is the evidence. Source: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra) 1.10.

cite.title: Yogabhāṣya (Vyāsa's commentary on the Yoga Sūtra)
cite.original:
sā ca saṃprabodhe pratyavamarśāt pratyayaviśeṣaḥ /
katham, sukham aham asvāpsam /
prasannaṃ me manaḥ /
prajñāṃ me viśāradīkaroti /
duḥkham aham asvāpsam /
styānaṃ me mano bhramaty anavasthitam gāḍhaṃ mūḍho 'ham asvāpsam /
gurūṇi me gātrāṇi /
klāntaṃ me cittam /
alasaṃ muṣitam iva tiṣṭhatīti /
sa khalv ayaṃ prabuddhasya pratyavamarśo na syād asati pratyayānubhave tadāśritāḥ smṛtayś ca tadviṣayā na syuḥ /
tasmāt pratyayaviśeṣo nidrā /
sā ca samādhāv itarapratyayavan niroddhavyeti
cite.paraphrase: Sleep is a particular kind of cognition (pratyaya-viśeṣa), because on waking it is recollected (pratyavamarśa). How? One says: 'I slept happily; my mind is clear; it makes my understanding lucid.' Or: 'I slept in pain (duḥkham); my mind, dull (styāna), wanders unsteady.' Or: 'I slept deeply, stupefied (mūḍha); my limbs are heavy; my mind is weary; it stays sluggish, as if robbed.' This recollection by one awake would not occur if there were no experience of a cognition, and the memories resting on it and having it as object would not occur either. So sleep is a particular cognition. And like the other cognitions, it is to be stilled in samādhi.

cite.title: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
cite.paraphrase: Indra, before reaching the gods, sees the flaw: if the body is adorned the reflection is adorned, if blind blind, and it perishes with the body. He returns; after thirty-two more years he is taught: 'the one who moves about happy in dreams is the self'. He sees the flaw again: though untouched by the body's defects, the dream-self seems to be struck and chased, to feel pain and to weep.

text: On the bus, one stranger laughing, another quietly crying. Friendliness toward the happy, compassion toward the suffering: the Yoga Sūtra gives each person an attitude. The sūtra has an attitude ready for each. Which one did the eyes go to first? (Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali 1.33)

cite.paraphrase: Compassion has as mark the occurring in the aspect of removing suffering; as function, not bearing others' suffering; as manifestation, non-cruelty; as proximate cause, seeing the helplessness of those overcome by suffering; its success is the stilling of cruelty, its failure the arising of sorrow. Gladness has as mark rejoicing; as function, non-envy; as manifestation, the removal of discontent; as proximate cause, seeing beings' success; success is the stilling of discontent, failure the arising of exhilaration (pahāsa). Equanimity has as mark the occurring in the aspect of neutrality toward beings; as function, seeing equality among beings; as manifestation, the stilling of resentment and favour; as proximate cause, seeing beings as owners of their kamma ("by whose wish will they be happy, or be freed from suffering, or not fall from the prosperity they have reached?"); success is the stilling of resentment and favour, failure the arising of the ignorant indifference of the household life. The common purpose of all four is pleasant abiding in insight and success in existence; the special purpose is the destruction of ill will and so on: loving-kindness for ill will, the others for cruelty, discontent and lust. The text quotes: "this is the escape from ill will, namely the liberation of mind by loving-kindness" and so for compassion (cruelty), gladness (discontent) and equanimity (lust). Each of the four has two enemies, near and far (continued on p. 319).

cite.paraphrase: When resentment toward the enemy has subsided, the mind occurs with loving-kindness toward him as toward the dear, the very dear friend and the neutral. Then, by developing loving-kindness again and again toward himself, the dear person, the neutral person and the enemy, and making the mind equal toward these four, he should break down the barriers (sīmasambheda). The mark: suppose he sits in one place with these three (dear, neutral, enemy) and himself as the fourth, and bandits come and say "give us one bhikkhu" for a blood-offering; if he thinks "let them take so-and-so", the barrier is not broken; even if he thinks "take me, not these three", it is not broken, because he wishes the good of one and not of the others. When among the four he sees no one to give the bandits and his mind is equal toward himself and the three, the barrier is broken. The ancients' verse: so long as he sees a difference among himself, the dear, the neutral and the hostile, though his mind is of good will toward beings, he is not called skilled in loving-kindness, one who gains it at will (nikāmalābhī); when the four barriers are broken down for the bhikkhu, he pervades the whole world with its gods with loving-kindness equally, and he whose barrier is no longer known is greatly better than the former. At the moment the barrier is broken the meditator gains the sign and access; then, developing that sign, he reaches absorption with little trouble in the way said for the earth kasiṇa: the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness (with five factors abandoned, five possessed, good in three ways, ten marks) and, continuing, the second and third in the fourfold count (the second, third and fourth in the fivefold) (continued on p. 308).

text: The degree is framed on the wall; 'what now?' remains. Nārada, learned in every branch of his day, tells Sanatkumāra: 'I know only the mantras, not the self'. Nārada had a whole wall of learning, and still came asking. What would the asking be? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.1.1-3)

cite.title: Chāndogya Upaniṣad
cite.paraphrase: Nārada approaches Sanatkumāra: he has studied the four Vedas, the itihāsa-purāṇa as the fifth Veda, the Veda of Vedas, the ancestral rites, reckoning, portents, chronology, dialectics, polity, the science of the gods, of brahman, of spirits, of rule, of the stars, of serpents and celestial beings; 'I know only the mantras, not the self; I have heard that one who knows the self crosses beyond sorrow; I am in sorrow; take me across.'

An old text puts it this way: The Satipaṭṭhāna asks one to see form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, each arising and passing away. (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta mn10:38)
Contemplating dhammas, one knows the five aggregates of clinging: such is form, such its arising, such its passing away; and likewise feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), formations (saṅkhārā) and consciousness (viññāṇa).
The sutta does not ask who anyone is. It watches what a person is made of come and go.
The Upaniṣads look for a self behind these parts; the sutta does not.
What arose and passed tonight?

cite.title: Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta
cite.original: 4.2. Dhammānupassanākhandhapabba Puna caparaṁ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu. Kathañca pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu: ‘iti rūpaṁ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā, iti vedanāya samudayo, iti vedanāya atthaṅgamo; iti saññā, iti saññāya samudayo, iti saññāya atthaṅgamo; iti saṅkhārā, iti saṅkhārānaṁ samudayo, iti saṅkhārānaṁ atthaṅgamo; iti viññāṇaṁ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti;
cite.paraphrase: Contemplation of dhammas, second section: the five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandha). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating dhammas with regard to the five aggregates of clinging. Here a monk (knows): 'such is form (rūpa), such its arising (samudaya), such its passing away (atthaṅgama); such is feeling (vedanā), such its arising, such its passing away; such is perception (saññā) …; such are formations (saṅkhārā) …; such is consciousness (viññāṇa), such its arising, such its passing away'.

Pulled three ways by work, family and a half-finished plan.

In this picture, someone is riding through the pull.
The Buddhist texts see no lasting rider, only the parts.
Who is holding the reins today?

cite.title: Dhammapada
cite.original: Puttā matthi dhanaṁ matthi, iti bālo vihaññati; Attā hi attano natthi, kuto puttā kuto dhanaṁ.
cite.paraphrase: 'I have sons, I have wealth': so the fool is troubled. For even oneself (attā) is not one's own (attā hi attano natthi): how then sons, how wealth?

text:
1. The scene (about 2 min). Points: Fifteen years in one role, and a letter ends it. Stay with the moment before judging it.
2. The teaching (about 2 min). Points: Ignorance (avidyā), the Yoga Sūtra says, takes the impermanent as permanent and the not-self as self. Source: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali 2.5.
3. Reading closely (about 2 min). Points: Ignorance (avidyā) is taking four things for their opposites: the impermanent for the permanent, the impure for the pure, the painful for the pleasant, the not-self (anātman) for the self (ātman). It heads the sūtra's list of afflictions. Say only what the passage says.
4. The link (about 2 min). Points: A role falls under two of its words: impermanent, and not-self.
5. Where the text stops (about 1 min). Points: Where the text stops: it describes what happens; it does not promise a result.
6. Close (about 1 min). Points: What was taken for permanent?

cite.title: Yoga Sūtra of Patañjali
cite.original: anityāśuciduḥkhānātmasu nityaśucisukhātmakhyātir avidyā
cite.paraphrase: Ignorance (avidyā) is taking the impermanent (anitya), the impure (aśuci), the painful (duḥkha) and the not-self (anātman) to be permanent (nitya), pure (śuci), pleasant (sukha) and self (ātman).

text: Writing the project summary, and deciding whose names go in. Praising oneself and hiding others' real virtues, the Tattvārtha says, bring in low-status karma (nīca gotra). The Jain text lists the moves a summary can make. Whose work is in it? (Tattvārthasūtra 6.25)

cite.title: Tattvārthasūtra
cite.original: parātma-nindā-praśaṃse sadasad guṇocchādanodbhāvane ca nīcairgotrasya
cite.paraphrase: Censuring others and praising oneself, and concealing others' real virtues and proclaiming one's own (unreal) ones are the inflow of low-status karma (nīca gotra).

text: A small slip at work grows larger with each replay. The mind quivers, hard to guard, the Dhammapada says; the discerning straighten it as a fletcher an arrow. The verse's picture: a bent arrow, and a fletcher straightening it. What would straightening be? (Dhammapada 33)

cite.title: Dhammapada
cite.original: Phandanaṁ capalaṁ cittaṁ, dūrakkhaṁ dunnivārayaṁ; Ujuṁ karoti medhāvī, usukārova tejanaṁ.
cite.paraphrase: The mind (citta) is quivering (phandana), unsteady (capala), hard to guard (dūrakkha), hard to restrain (dunnivāraya); the discerning one makes it straight, as a fletcher makes an arrow straight.

text:
Notification, tab, another tab, and the evening is gone.
An old text puts it this way: A mind led by the roving senses, the Gītā says, carries off one's wisdom like wind taking a ship on water. (Bhagavad Gītā 2.67)
Kṛṣṇa: when the mind (manas) is led along by the roving senses, it carries off one's wisdom (prajñā), as the wind carries off a ship on the water.
Each tab is a gust in the verse's picture.
Where did the wind take it tonight?

cite.title: Bhagavad Gītā
cite.original:
indriyāṇāṃ hi caratāṃ yanmano'nuvidhīyate|
tadasya harati prajñāṃ vāyurnāvamivāmbhasi
cite.paraphrase: Kṛṣṇa: for when the mind (manas) is led along by the roving senses, it carries off his wisdom (prajñā), as the wind carries off a ship on the water.

text:
1. The scene (about 2 min). Points: A week of choosing between two options, and still no choice. Stay with the moment before judging it.
2. The teaching (about 2 min). Points: Let go of the before, let go of the after, let go of the middle, the Dhammapada says, going beyond becoming. Source: Dhammapada 348.
3. Reading closely (about 2 min). Points: Three times the verse says let go: of the before, of the after, of the middle. Then it names going beyond existence (bhava), with a mind freed everywhere. Say only what the passage says.
4. The link (about 2 min). Points: What was said before, what might come after, the choosing in the middle: the verse says the same to each.
5. Where the text stops (about 1 min). Points: The verse ends on its own goal: with the mind freed everywhere, the Dhammapada says, one does not come again to birth and ageing. That is the text's goal in its own words; this post promises nothing.
6. Close (about 1 min). Points: Which of the three is loudest?

cite.title: Dhammapada
cite.original: Muñca pure muñca pacchato, Majjhe muñca bhavassa pāragū; Sabbattha vimuttamānaso, Na punaṁ jātijaraṁ upehisi.
cite.paraphrase: Let go of the before, let go of the after, let go of the middle, going beyond existence (bhava); with a mind freed everywhere, you will not again come to birth and ageing.

text: A dream hangs around all through breakfast. The second quarter, the Māṇḍūkya says, is dream: inward-knowing, enjoying a world set apart. The Upaniṣad does not read the dream. It gives dream its own station, facing inward. Where is that world now? (Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad 4)

cite.title: Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad
cite.original: svaprasthāno 'ntaḥprajñaḥ saptāṅga ekonaviṃśatimukhaḥ praviviktabhuktaijaso dvitīyaḥ pādaḥ
cite.paraphrase: The second quarter is the brilliant one (taijasa): its station is dream (svapna-sthāna); it is inward-knowing (antaḥprajña), has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and is the enjoyer of the separated (praviviktabhuj).

text:
[on screen: A dream: the old school corridor opens onto the office.] A dream: the old school corridor opens onto the office.
[on screen: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.9-14] There is an old text that says it plainly. In dream, says the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, one breaks up this world and builds it again by one's own light.
Here is what the passage says, closely: Dream is the junction between this world and the other. There one takes material from this world, breaks it up, builds it again and dreams by one's own radiance. No roads are there; the dreamer creates them.
The pieces came from waking life; the building was the dreamer's own.
Where the text stops: it says what it says; reading it into your own day is left to you.
[on screen: What did the dream borrow from the day?] What did the dream borrow from the day?

cite.title: Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad
cite.paraphrase: The person has two states — this world and the other — and a third, the junction, dream. In dream, taking material from this all-containing world, he himself breaks it up and builds it again, and dreams by his own radiance; there the person becomes his own light (svayaṃjyotiḥ). There are no chariots, teams or roads there, no joys or pools, but he creates them, for he is the creator. People see his playground; no one sees him.

text:
[on screen: Cooking rice for four, out of habit, in a flat for one.] Cooking rice for four, out of habit, in a flat for one.
[on screen: Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.10.1] There is an old text that says it plainly. It is a vow, the Taittirīya says, never to turn anyone away from one's dwelling; so gather plenty of food.
Here is what the passage says, closely: It is a vow: not to turn anyone away from one's dwelling. So by whatever means, one should obtain much food, and they say of such a person, 'food is made ready for him'.
The vow gives the extra a use: food ready for whoever comes.
Where the text stops: it says what it says; reading it into your own day is left to you.
[on screen: Whose plate might it be?] Whose plate might it be?

cite.title: Taittirīya Upaniṣad
cite.original: na kañcana vasatau pratyācakṣīta | tadvratam | tasmādyayā kayā ca vidhayā bahvannaṃ prāpnuyāt | arādhyasmā annamityācakṣate | etadvai mukhato'nnaṃ rāddham | mukhato'smā annaṃ rādhyate | etadvai madhyato'nnaṃ rāddham | madhyato'smā annaṃ rādhyate | etadvā antato'nnaṃ rāddham | antato'smā annaṃ rādhyate
cite.paraphrase: It is a vow: not to turn anyone away from one's dwelling. Therefore by whatever means one may, one should obtain much food; they say to such a person "food is made ready for him." If this food is prepared at the front, food is prepared for him at the front; if in the middle, food is prepared for him in the middle; if at the end, food is prepared for him at the end.

text:
1. The scene (about 2 min). Points: A contact list of four hundred names, scrolled to the end. Stay with the moment before judging it.
2. The teaching (about 2 min). Points: If one finds a wise companion of good conduct, the Dhammapada says, walk on with them, glad and mindful. Source: Dhammapada 328.
3. Reading closely (about 2 min). Points: If one gets a wise companion who fares with one, of good conduct and steadfast, one should fare with him, overcoming all dangers (parissaya), glad-minded and mindful. Say only what the passage says.
4. The link (about 2 min). Points: The verse sets a measure for company, not a number: one wise companion.
5. Where the text stops (about 1 min). Points: Where the text stops: it says what it says; reading it into your own day is left to you.
6. Close (about 1 min). Points: Who would that one be?

cite.title: Dhammapada
cite.original: Sace labhetha nipakaṁ sahāyaṁ, Saddhiṁ caraṁ sādhuvihāridhīraṁ; Abhibhuyya sabbāni parissayāni, Careyya tenattamano satīmā.
cite.paraphrase: If one gets a wise companion, one who fares with one, is of good conduct and steadfast, overcoming all dangers (parissaya), one should fare with him, glad-minded and mindful (satīmant).

text: Asked 'who are you?', the answers start with name and job. The Taittirīya describes five selves, each within the last: of food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss. Its list has no name or job; it starts at the body. What comes after the job? (Taittirīya Upaniṣad ch2)

cite.title: Taittirīya Upaniṣad
cite.paraphrase: The Brahmānandavallī (2.1.1-2.9.1): it defines brahman as truth, knowledge, infinite and traces emergence from the self (2.1); gives the five selves made of food, breath, mind, understanding and bliss, each within the last and person-shaped, with brahman as the tail and support of the innermost (2.1-2.5); asks whether the ignorant or the knower reaches that world, and gives the emergence and entry of the one who wished to be many (2.6); the essence and fearlessness (2.7); the scale of bliss by hundredfold steps up to brahman (2.8); and the fearlessness of the one who knows the bliss of brahman (2.9).

text:
[on screen: A choice between the safe offer and the one that feels right.] A choice between the safe offer and the one that feels right.
[on screen: Katha Upaniṣad 1.2.1-2] There is an old text that says it plainly. The good and the pleasant differ, the Kaṭha says; both come to a person, and the wise tell them apart.
Here is what the passage says, closely: Yama tells Naciketas: the good (śreyas) is one thing, the pleasant (preyas) another; both bind a person. Both come to a person; the wise one examines and distinguishes them, and prefers the good. The fool chooses the pleasant for getting and keeping.
Neither comes labelled; the Upaniṣad asks that they be examined first.
Where the text stops: it says what it says; reading it into your own day is left to you.
[on screen: Which is which?] Which is which?

cite.title: Katha Upaniṣad
cite.original: śreyaś ca preyaś ca manuṣyam etas tau samparītya vivinakti dhīraḥ | śreyo hi dhīro 'bhi preyaso vṛṇīte preyo mando yogakṣemād vṛṇīte
cite.paraphrase: The good (śreyas) is one thing, the pleasant (preyas) another; both bind a person with different aims. Good comes to one who takes the good; one who chooses the pleasant misses the goal. Both come to a person; the wise one examines and distinguishes them; the wise prefers the good to the pleasant; the fool chooses the pleasant for the sake of getting and keeping (yogakṣema).
